slots.title: September housing starts at 1.22M miss 1.3M est.
slots.body:
September housing starts: **1.22M** (annualized).

Consensus: **1.30M**.
Prior month: **1.29M**.

Starts fell **5.2%** month over month.

Economists had expected a **+1.9%** monthly change; August was **−5.9%**.

The release counts new residential construction starts — a read on homebuilding and related demand for materials and jobs.

What part of the housing pipeline do you watch first — permits or starts?

slots.title: Building permits 1.4M edge past 1.39M estimate
slots.body:
September building permits: **1.40M** (annualized).

Estimate: **1.39M**.
Prior: **1.40M**.

Permits down **0.2%** month over month.

Forecast had been **−0.7%**; August was **−2.1%**.

Permits are approvals to begin construction — they often lead starts by a month or two.

Same release window as housing starts (Sep), both out **Oct 20** at 12:30 ET.

Do you treat a small level beat and a still-negative MoM as mixed, or one clear signal?

slots.title: JPMorgan commits $5B to security-linked firms
slots.body:
JPMorgan Chase pledged **$5 billion** in equity capital.

Target areas: U.S. **national security**, **defense technology**, and **critical supply chains**.

Reported **Oct 20** — a corporate policy and capital-allocation headline, not a government spending print.

Same session, the Dow closed up **1.0%** at **52,495.88** and the S&P 500 up **0.3%** at **7,711.06**; no single index line in the feed ties those moves to this announcement.

How much do you separate big-bank “strategic equity” programs from straight lending or M&A?

slots.title: GM down 6.8% after 2027 outlook
slots.body:
$GM closed at 77.09, down 6.8% (−5.66) on the session.

Q3 EPS came in at 3.70 vs 3.69 estimated; revenue at about $50.0B vs roughly $48.8B estimated.

Reporting pointed to the company flagging a rocky 2027 as part of why the stock sold off after the print.

The $RUT rose 1.7% while consumer cyclical names were mixed on the day.

slots.title: U.S. session recap — Oct. 20, 2026
slots.body:
The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 1.0% to 52,495.88 (+529.85 points), leading the major U.S. benchmarks after a choppy session.

The S&P 500 added 0.3% to 7,711.06; the Russell 2000 outpaced large caps with a 1.7% gain to 2,773.62.

The Nasdaq Composite was essentially unchanged, down less than 0.1% to 26,424.82, as several large technology names closed lower.

The CBOE Volatility Index fell 6.1% to 17.31, the lowest close among the session’s index readings in the injected tape.

September housing starts printed at 1.221 million (annual rate), below the 1.3 million consensus; building permits were 1.4 million vs 1.39 million estimated, with housing starts down 5.2% month over month.

Healthcare was the strongest Nasdaq sector in the dataset, averaging about +2.0%; real estate averaged +1.4% and financial services about +1.1%.

Communication services averaged about −0.5%, consumer defensive about −0.8%, and energy about −0.8% among Nasdaq sectors.

Among megacaps, $UNH rose 3.0% to 419.26; $TSLA gained 1.5% to 373.71; $TSM added 1.2% to 425.08.

$META fell 1.6% to 694.25, $GOOGL −1.1% to 340.27, $AAPL −1.0% to 339.50, and $NFLX −1.7% to 68.69 despite Q3 EPS 0.87 vs 0.82 estimated and revenue near $12.87B.

Earnings drove wide single-name swings:
- $EFX +11.3%
- $MMM +5.8%
- $NOC +4.6%
- $MSCI +5.0%

while $GM −6.8% and $GE −3.7% despite beats on EPS and revenue in the calendar data.

$SPCX closed −0.1% at 147.79 after reporting EPS 0.35 vs 0.13 estimated and revenue about $14.6B vs roughly $12.9B estimated; coverage in the feed noted the company’s first quarterly profit narrative.

Cross-asset moves were modest: gold futures −0.2% to 4,133.20, Brent crude +1.5% to 110.45, the dollar proxy $UUP −0.3% to 28.90, and bitcoin −0.3% to about 82,680.79.

Overseas indexes in the package were mixed into the U.S. close window: Japan’s Nikkei 225 +1.2%, Germany proxy +1.0%, FTSE 100 −0.3%, Hang Seng −0.2%.

Latest Treasury snapshot in the feed (dated 2026-10-16) showed the 10-year yield at 5.1% and the 2s10s spread at 0.35 percentage points.

slots.title: Jobless claims due Thursday 12:30 ET
slots.body:
U.S. jobless claims hit the wire Thursday, Oct. 22, at 12:30 p.m.
ET.

Initial claims (new filings for unemployment benefits) carry a 200,000 estimate versus 199,000 the prior week.

Continuing claims (people still receiving benefits) are modeled at 1.72 million, up from 1.71 million.

The four-week average for initial claims is estimated at 200,000; the prior reading was 198.5.

The release is tagged high impact in the calendar and is one of the few labor prints still published every week.

It measures layoff pace and how quickly idled workers move off the rolls.

Do you treat this as a leading read on hiring, or mostly noise week to week?

slots.title: Three PMI readings Friday 1:45 p.m.
slots.body:
Three S&P Global PMI releases are scheduled for Friday, Oct. 23, at 1:45 p.m.
ET.

Composite PMI (whole economy) — estimate 57.6 points, prior 58.4.

Services PMI — estimate 58.0, prior 58.8.

Manufacturing PMI — estimate 55.5, prior 55.9.

PMI is a monthly business survey: scores above 50 mean expansion, below 50 mean contraction.

All three are listed as medium impact and use index points, not percent change.

That batch closes the Oct. 19–23 calendar window after a week that already included September housing starts and building permits on Oct. 20.

Which sector PMI do you read as the best pulse on U.S. demand?
